There are cities that exist only in the margins of history—places where the past lingers like a half-remembered dream. Some are lost beneath the weight of time, their ruins swallowed by the earth or reduced to legends whispered by travelers who dare to seek them. But then there are the ones that persist, not as ruins, but as living things, breathing with the slow, deliberate pulse of forgotten traditions. Among these, the Whispering Gardens of Veythar stand as a testament to what happens when memory refuses to die.

Veythar was once a thriving metropolis, a city of towering spires and bustling markets where merchants from across the known world traded in spices, silk, and secrets. Its name was lost to the sands of time, but its legends endure. The gardens, nestled within the heart of the old city, were said to have been planted by a sorcerer-king who sought to bind the essence of the land itself to the earth. The trees grew in unnatural patterns—some twisted like the arms of ancient guardians, others forming intricate labyrinths that seemed to shift with the wind. The flowers bloomed in hues that defied nature, their petals shimmering with colors that shifted between dawn and dusk. And then there were the whispers.

They came at first as gentle murmurs, the kind of sound you might hear in a crowded market, but with a quality of familiarity. A voice would speak in a language no one recognized, yet each word carried the weight of a thousand voices. The first time I heard it, I was standing beneath an ancient willow, its branches heavy with fruit that glowed faintly in the moonlight. The words were simple: *"You are not alone."* I laughed, thinking it was the wind, but the next morning, the same voice spoke again, this time in my dreams. I woke with the taste of something sweet on my lips, and when I looked at my hands, they were covered in petals that had fallen from the trees.

The gardens were not open to the public. The city’s guards, if they still existed, were said to be more like guardians than men—tall, silent figures with eyes that seemed to see beyond the veil of the ordinary. Those who ventured into the Whispering Gardens were never the same. Some returned with stories of conversations with the trees, of being guided through paths that led to hidden chambers where the walls pulsed with light. Others never returned at all, their bodies found months later, their faces frozen in expressions of awe or terror. The whispers grew louder, more insistent, as if the gardens themselves were learning the names of those who dared to listen.
